- **meditation-on-the-law (Ps 1:1-3 parallel)** — 1:8 (The meditation-on-the-law framework at Josh 1:8 parallels Ps 1:1-3's near-verbatim framework. The Exod 3:5 burning-bush parallel + holy-ground command + Joshua's worship-reception are the chapter's structural-anchors for the typological framework.)

## Per-chapter highlights

### Chapter 1 — ‘Be Strong and of a Good Courage’: The LORD Commissions Joshua

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, inheritance

After Moses' death, the LORD speaks directly to Joshua and gives the foundational charge for entering the land. The five-fold "be strong and of a good courage" formula completes its installation across Deut 31 and Joshua 1, spoken by Moses, by the LORD, and finally by the people themselves to Joshua. The chapter is the narrative-prophetic culmination of the Joshua- succession typological framework that Num 27 first installed.

### Chapter 2 — Rahab and the Spies: ‘The LORD Your God, He Is God in Heaven Above’

*status:* draft
*themes:* prophetic-call, covenant, holiness

Joshua sends two spies to Jericho; they lodge with Rahab the harlot, who hides them under flax-stalks on her rooftop. Rahab's confession at 2:9-11 — "the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath" — installs the chapter's theological center: a Canaanite woman declaring full monotheistic recognition of YHWH. The chapter has substantial NT reception: Hebrews 11:31 (faith-paradigm), James 2:25 (faith-and-works), and Matthew 1:5 (messianic genealogy inclusion).

### Chapter 3 — Crossing the Jordan: The Ark, the Priests, and the Waters Stood Up at Adam

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

Israel breaks camp at Shittim and comes to the Jordan; the priests bearing the ark of the covenant lead the people, and when their feet touch the river's brim the waters cut off and stand up in a heap at the city Adam upstream. The new generation crosses on dry ground — narratively echoing the first generation's Red Sea crossing under Moses, with the chapter opening the two-chapter Joshua 3-4 unit whose memorial-stones framework follows.

### Chapter 4 — The Twelve Stones: ‘When Your Children Shall Ask in Time to Come’

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

The Jordan-crossing's structural-completion. Twelve men, one from each tribe, take twelve stones from the riverbed and pitch them at Gilgal as a perpetual memorial; Joshua sets up a parallel twelve stones in the riverbed where the priests stood. The chapter installs the intergenerational-memory pedagogy framework ("when your children shall ask"), explicitly paralleling the Jordan crossing to the Red Sea crossing, and registers the LORD's magnification of Joshua before all Israel.

### Chapter 5 — Gilgal Circumcision, Passover, and the Captain of the LORD's Host

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, holiness, prophetic-call

The new generation enters the land as a covenant-marked people: the Gilgal circumcision rolls away the reproach of Egypt, the Passover at Gilgal closes the manna era, and Joshua encounters the captain of the LORD's host outside Jericho with a drawn sword and the same holy-ground command Moses received at the burning bush. The chapter installs three theologically-substantive units in immediate succession.

### Chapter 6 — The Fall of Jericho: ‘By Faith the Walls of Jericho Fell Down’

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, holiness

The seven-day march around Jericho — six days of one circuit, and on the seventh day seven circuits with the priests blowing the trumpets and the people shouting — culminates in the walls falling down flat and the herem framework's execution, with Rahab and her household alone preserved per the Josh 2 oath. Hebrews 11:30 reads the chapter as the conquest's faith-paradigm, paired with Heb 11:31's reading of Rahab.

### Chapter 7 — Achan and the Defeat at Ai: ‘Israel Hath Sinned’

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, holiness, prophetic-call

Achan violates the herem at Jericho, Israel is defeated at Ai, and the LORD declares ‘Israel hath sinned’ — singular, collective-juridical. Achan is identified by lot through tribe, family, and household; he confesses; he is stoned and burned in the Valley of Achor, where the framework Hosea 2:15 will later read as the door-of-hope. The chapter is the OT's hardest single installation of the covenantal-collective-responsibility framework.

### Chapter 8 — Ai Retaken + the Gerizim/Ebal Covenant Ceremony Executed

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, holiness

Israel returns to Ai with the LORD's ambush instructions and takes the city; the king is hanged on a tree until eventide and taken down before sundown per the Deut 21:22-23 framework. Joshua then leads the people to Mount Ebal, builds the altar of unhewn stones, inscribes the law, and executes the Gerizim/Ebal antiphonal blessing-and-curse ceremony Moses had commanded — framework's cross-session completion across four sessions of the project's drafting work.

### Chapter 9 — The Gibeonite Deception and the Oath That Held

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, holiness

The Gibeonites disguise themselves as travelers from a far country with moldy bread and worn garments; Israel's leaders swear a peace-covenant without consulting the LORD. Three days later the deception is discovered, but the oath binds Israel — the Gibeonites become hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and the altar. The covenant's juridical force is later tested at 2 Samuel 21:1-9 when Saul's violation triggers a three-year famine in David's reign.

### Chapter 10 — The Sun Stood Still: Israel Defends Gibeon, the Southern Campaign Closes

*status:* published
*themes:* prophetic-call, covenant, holiness

The five-king Amorite coalition attacks Gibeon as punishment for the Joshua-Gibeonite covenant; Israel marches all night to relieve the city. The LORD throws great hailstones; Joshua prays for the sun to stand still upon Gibeon, and the Book of Jasher records that it did so "about a whole day." The chapter then narrates the southern campaign's systematic conquest, closing with seven cities and the framework's "the LORD fought for Israel" register.

### Chapter 11 — The Northern Campaign + ‘And the Land Rested from War’

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, rest

Jabin king of Hazor gathers the northern coalition, and the LORD delivers them slain before Israel at the waters of Merom; Joshua destroys Hazor by fire, the cities of the kings are taken, and the Anakim are cut off from the mountains. The chapter closes with the framework Hebrews 4:8-11 reads typologically — Joshua took the whole land and the land rested from war — registering the rest-that-is-not-the-final-rest.

### Chapter 12 — The King-Summary: Thirty-One Defeated — Part I Closes

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

The conquest-narrative's structural-closing inventory. Two trans-Jordan kings (Sihon and Og) defeated under Moses; thirty- one cis-Jordan kings defeated under Joshua, enumerated city by city from Jericho through the southern, central, and northern conquests. The chapter's form-as-substance discipline registers the numerical comprehensiveness as the framework's theological point and closes Joshua's Part I — the conquest narrative — before the land-allotment chapters open at Joshua 13.

### Chapter 13 — ‘There Remaineth Yet Very Much Land’: The Allotment Begins

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

The LORD addresses Joshua now old and stricken in years: much land remains to be possessed, and the inheritance must be divided. The chapter opens the land-allotment block (Part II of Joshua, chapters 13-21) with the eastern tribes' inheritance review — Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh receiving Moses' prior trans-Jordan allotment — and the structural-reminder that Levi has no territorial inheritance because the LORD is their portion.

### Chapter 14 — Caleb at Eighty-Five: ‘He Wholly Followed the LORD’

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

The cis-Jordan allotment opens with Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal heads casting lots. Caleb of Judah approaches Joshua and recalls Moses' Kadesh-promise from forty-five years earlier: the LORD swore him the land where his feet had trodden because he had wholly followed the LORD. Now eighty-five, Caleb requests Hebron — still the giant-Anakim mountain country — and Joshua blesses him with the inheritance Num 14:24 had promised.

### Chapter 15 — Judah's Allotment: Borders, Caleb-Othniel-Achsah, and the Jebusites Who Remained

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

Judah receives the southern allotment — from Edom and the Salt Sea east to the Mediterranean west, with a detailed border description from family to family. Caleb conquers Hebron; offers his daughter Achsah to whoever takes Kirjath-sepher; Othniel takes it and Achsah requests the upper and nether springs. The chapter closes with the framework-honest notation that the children of Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem.

### Chapter 16 — Ephraim's Allotment: Joseph's Border + the Canaanites in Gezer Who Remained

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

The lot of the children of Joseph falls from Jordan by Jericho westward; Ephraim's specific territory is detailed within the broader Joseph allotment. The chapter is brief — a transitional block between Judah's southern allotment (Josh 15) and Manasseh's allotment with the Zelophehad-daughters narrative (Josh 17). The chapter closes with the candid notation that Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites at Gezer.

### Chapter 17 — Manasseh's Allotment: Zelophehad's Daughters Receive Their Inheritance

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

Manasseh's allotment opens; Machir's east-Jordan inheritance is noted as already given; six male-line clans receive cis-Jordan portions. Then Zelophehad's five daughters — named again, as in Num 27 and Num 36 — come before Eleazar, Joshua, and the princes, and "according to the commandment of the LORD" he gives them an inheritance among their father's brethren. Manasseh's borders follow; the chapter closes with the children of Joseph's complaint about having only one lot and Joshua's response promising the mountain even against iron chariots.

### Chapter 18 — Shiloh, the Tabernacle, and Benjamin's Allotment Between Judah and Joseph

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

The whole congregation assembles at Shiloh and sets up the tabernacle there — the cultic center for the next several centuries. Seven tribes still lack their inheritance; Joshua asks how long they will be slack, commissions three-men-per-tribe to survey the land, and casts lots at Shiloh before the LORD. Benjamin's allotment falls first — geographically wedged between Judah on the south and Joseph on the north, including Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, and Jerusalem-as-Jebusi.

### Chapter 19 — The Remaining Six Tribes — and Joshua's Inheritance at Timnath-serah

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

The remaining six lots fall at Shiloh — Simeon (within Judah's too-large portion), Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan (whose territory proves insufficient, so they migrate north and take Leshem, renaming it Dan). The allotment closes with Joshua himself receiving his inheritance last: Timnath-serah in mount Ephraim, the city he asked for and then built. The chapter's closing-formula names Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the heads of the fathers at Shiloh before the LORD — "so they made an end of dividing the country."

### Chapter 20 — Six Cities of Refuge Appointed: The Promise Made by Moses Now Made Real

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

The LORD instructs Joshua to appoint the cities of refuge "whereof I spake unto you by the hand of Moses." Three cis-Jordan cities are named — Kedesh in Naphtali, Shechem in Ephraim, Hebron in Judah — and the three trans-Jordan cities Moses had already set apart at Deut 4:41-43 are reconfirmed: Bezer (Reuben), Ramoth- gilead (Gad), Golan in Bashan (Manasseh). The institution is open to "all the children of Israel, and for the stranger that sojourneth among them." The Mosaic instruction reaches narrative- execution.

### Chapter 21 — Forty-Eight Levitical Cities — and 'There Failed Not Ought of Any Good Thing'

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

The heads of the Levites come to Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal heads at Shiloh and receive their forty-eight cities-with-suburbs, distributed across all twelve tribal territories. The six cities of refuge appointed in Josh 20 are each marked here as Levitical cities — Hebron the first Aaronic city, Shechem, Kedesh, Golan, Bezer, Ramoth-gilead each carried as "a city of refuge for the slayer." The chapter closes with the book's most explicit promise- fulfillment declaration: "There failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass."

### Chapter 22 — The Altar at the Jordan: A Crisis Resolved Through Dialogue, Not War

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

Joshua dismisses the two-and-a-half eastern tribes home with blessing and warning. At the Jordan crossing they build a great altar; the western tribes interpret it as apostasy and gather for civil war. Phinehas son of Eleazar leads ten princes to investigate; the eastern tribes explain the altar is a witness, not for sacrifice — built out of fear that Jordan-as-border might be used to exclude their children from "any part in the LORD." Phinehas accepts; war is averted; the altar is named Ed (witness).

### Chapter 23 — Joshua's First Farewell: 'Not One Thing Hath Failed of All the Good Things'

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

Joshua, "old and stricken in age," summons Israel's elders, heads, judges, and officers for his first farewell address. He recalls the LORD as the one who fought for Israel; charges them to keep the book of the law of Moses, to cleave unto the LORD, and to shun the remnant nations and their gods; warns that intermarriage with the remnant will make the remnant into snares, traps, scourges, and thorns; declares "I am going the way of all the earth" and repeats the Josh 21:45 totality-formula in personal voice: "not one thing hath failed of all the good things which the LORD your God spake."

### Chapter 24 — Covenant at Shechem — Joshua's Death — Joseph's Bones Laid to Rest

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

Joshua gathers all the tribes at Shechem and delivers a first- person-divine-voice historical recap from Terah to the conquest. "Choose you this day whom ye will serve... as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." A three-fold affirmation is sealed with a witness-stone under the oak. The chapter closes with three deaths: Joshua at 110 in Timnath-serah; Joseph's bones laid to rest at Shechem after four centuries; Eleazar son of Aaron — the post- Mosaic priestly and military generation formally closed.
